title: Which Genie Do You Need?
brief: You are given twelve real questions from a Meridian shared inbox. Sort each into one
Genie One    — a business question over data that already exists
Genie Agent  — needs a curated domain built first
Genie Code   — someone needs help writing or fixing code
Not a data question at all
Then take the single hardest one and list every business definition that would have to
be settled before ANY tool could answer it correctly.
Compare your list with a colleague's. The disagreement is the finding — if two people
who know the business cannot agree what a question means, no agent will do better.
review: Every question lands in a bucket, with a reason rather than a label.
At least one is correctly called 'not a data question'.
The definitions list for the hardest question names a disagreement, not just terms.
The learner noticed that 'needs a curated domain' is a judgement about effort, not a property of the question.

inputs.title: The twelve questions, as they arrived in the inbox
rows: 1. "What's our AUM?"  — Head of Distribution, no other context
2. "Can someone pull the flows for the Northeast last quarter?"
3. "Why did the Q2 board pack show a different AUM to the client statements?"
4. "I need a list of every client in California with more than $5m."
5. "The reconciliation job is failing with a null pointer on line 214."
6. "How did the multi-asset strategies do against benchmark last year?"
8. "Can you add a column to the custodian feed for accrued income?"
9. "What were net sales in FY2026 Q3, excluding exchanges?"
10. "Is it worth opening an office in Denver?"
11. "How much do we manage for the Hartmann family?"
12. "Give me the same as last month but for fixed income."
Four buckets: Genie One, Genie Agent, Genie Code, Not a data question.
Two are deliberately unfair. Number 7 has no definition of underperforming;
number 10 is a business judgement no data answers. Number 11 looks simple and
is not: 'the Hartmann family' has no equivalent in the data at all.
